items.title: Urban Trees and Unequal Cooling
items.passage:
Trees can make a city street more comfortable on a hot day. Their shade reduces the solar energy reaching pavement, while evaporation from leaves transfers some heat into water vapor. These mechanisms help explain why a tree-lined block may feel different from a nearby street with little vegetation.
However, simply counting trees is an incomplete measure of the cooling people experience. A young tree with a narrow crown may offer little shade, whereas a mature tree can cover a large pedestrian area. Placement also matters. Trees in an inaccessible courtyard provide different benefits from those shading a busy bus stop. Measures of canopy cover and the location of shade therefore complement tree counts.
Maintenance introduces another complication. Trees need suitable soil, water and protection from damage. Planting many seedlings without supporting their survival may produce impressive initial statistics but little lasting cooling. Some neighborhoods face greater barriers to maintenance, including limited space beneath sidewalks and fewer resources for watering.
Urban planning consequently involves more than choosing a numerical planting target. Residents can identify routes and gathering places where shade is most needed, while arborists assess which species can survive local conditions. A program that considers survival, canopy growth and everyday access is more likely to distribute benefits fairly than one evaluated only by the number of planting events.

items.prompt: What is the passage mainly concerned with?
options: The historical origin of community volunteer organizations

A claim that all old appliances should be replaced immediately
The interacting factors that affect whether repair is worthwhile
items.explanation: The passage considers price, design, knowledge and environmental trade-offs.
items.title: The Economics of Repair
items.passage:
When a household appliance stops working, replacing it may appear simpler than repairing it. Yet the decision depends on more than the price of a replacement. Repair involves diagnosis, skilled labor and access to compatible parts. If one of these is difficult to obtain, even a minor fault can make an otherwise serviceable product expensive to fix.
Design influences this calculation. A casing held together with accessible screws can be opened without destroying it. A sealed assembly may require replacing several working components along with the failed one. Manufacturers also influence repair through the availability of manuals and spare parts. The same technical failure can therefore have different economic consequences in differently designed products.
Community repair events address some of these barriers. Volunteers may help diagnose faults or demonstrate a simple procedure. Such events can reduce uncertainty and increase practical knowledge, but they cannot guarantee that every item is safe or economical to repair. Electrical hazards and unavailable components still impose limits.
The wider significance of repair includes the materials and energy used to manufacture replacements. Keeping an appliance in use can postpone those demands. Nevertheless, an unusually inefficient old appliance may create a different trade-off. Evaluating repair requires attention to the particular product and its continued operation, rather than assuming that either repair or replacement is always the better choice.

lower.prompt: What is the passage’s central claim?
options: All commercial transactions create lasting friendships
The most crowded market is necessarily the most inclusive

Attendance totals alone reveal a market’s social success
lower.explanation: The argument combines repeated interaction, design and barriers.
lower.title: How a Market Becomes a Meeting Place
lower.passage:
A weekly market is a place to exchange goods, but its social role may extend beyond transactions. People who arrive at similar times repeatedly encounter the same sellers and customers. Brief conversations about products can develop into recognition and, eventually, relationships that persist outside the market itself.
The physical arrangement of the space influences these encounters. Benches near food stalls allow visitors to remain after shopping. Narrow passages may increase contact, but overcrowding can discourage people who find the space uncomfortable. A successful social space does not simply force the greatest number of people into the smallest area.
Researchers studying markets therefore observe how people use them rather than relying only on attendance totals. A large crowd might consist mainly of customers who leave quickly. A smaller market could support longer visits and more repeated interactions. Interviews can reveal whether participants feel welcome, while observation can show which groups actually use particular areas.
Markets are not automatically inclusive. High prices, limited opening hours or inaccessible entrances may exclude some residents. Organizers who want a market to function as a neighborhood meeting place must consider these barriers alongside commercial success. The market’s social contribution emerges from patterns of participation, and those patterns depend partly on deliberate decisions about space, access and scheduling.

higher.title: Signals in an Ice Core
higher.passage:
Ice accumulating in a cold region can preserve evidence of past environments. Snow becomes compressed beneath later snowfall, and small bubbles of air may eventually be trapped within the ice. A core drilled through the accumulated layers offers a sequence of samples rather than a single snapshot of the past.
Different features answer different questions. Air bubbles can preserve samples of an earlier atmosphere. Particles such as dust may reflect changes in winds or exposed land surfaces. Certain chemical properties of the ice provide clues about the conditions under which the original snow formed. Interpreting these clues requires understanding how each signal entered the ice.
The depth of a sample is related to its age, but the relationship is not necessarily uniform. Layers become compressed, snowfall rates change and flowing ice can deform older material. Researchers combine layer counting, known events and physical models to build an age estimate. They also report uncertainty rather than assigning every depth a perfectly precise date.
A further distinction concerns the age of the trapped air. Air can continue moving through porous snow before the surrounding material becomes sealed ice. Consequently, the air in a bubble may be younger than the ice enclosing it. Careful interpretation therefore involves comparing several records and their dating assumptions, not treating every signal at the same depth as exactly simultaneous.

Ice accumulating in a cold region can preserve evidence of past environments. Snow becomes compressed beneath later snowfall, and small bubbles of air may eventually be trapped within the ice. A core drilled through the accumulated layers offers a sequence of samples rather than a single snapshot of the past.
Different features answer different questions. Air bubbles can preserve samples of an earlier atmosphere. Particles such as dust may reflect changes in winds or exposed land surfaces. Certain chemical properties of the ice provide clues about the conditions under which the original snow formed. Interpreting these clues requires understanding how each signal entered the ice.
The depth of a sample is related to its age, but the relationship is not necessarily uniform. Layers become compressed, snowfall rates change and flowing ice can deform older material. Researchers combine layer counting, known events and physical models to build an age estimate. They also report uncertainty rather than assigning every depth a perfectly precise date.
A further distinction concerns the age of the trapped air. Air can continue moving through porous snow before the surrounding material becomes sealed ice. Consequently, the air in a bubble may be younger than the ice enclosing it. Careful interpretation therefore involves comparing several records and their dating assumptions, not treating every signal at the same depth as exactly simultaneous.

items.title: The Cost of Waiting in a Queue

stimulus.title: The Cost of Waiting in a Queue
stimulus.script:
Queues are often described simply by their length, but two queues containing the same number of people can feel very different. One may move steadily, while the other gives little indication of progress. Information about the process influences how people experience the wait.
Suppose a student needs advice at a busy service desk. If the student knows roughly when their turn will come, they may be able to read or complete another task. Without that information, they might feel obliged to watch the desk continuously. The number of minutes can be identical, yet the uncertainty and the opportunity cost differ.
Researchers must also consider fairness. A system that speeds up the average wait may still be unpopular if people cannot understand why later arrivals are being served first. Sometimes different kinds of requests genuinely require separate staff. Explaining that arrangement can prevent a reasonable process from appearing arbitrary.
This does not mean that communication can solve every problem. If too few staff are available, a clear sign will not create the missing capacity. Improvements may require both operational changes and better information. Studying a queue therefore involves its actual movement, the decisions behind it and the experience of the people who are waiting.

items.title: Seeing Colors in Different Light

stimulus.title: Seeing Colors in Different Light
stimulus.script:
You may have chosen clothing in a shop and found that its color looked different outdoors. The material did not necessarily change during the walk home. What changed was the light reaching it and, therefore, the light it reflected toward your eyes.
White-looking light can contain different mixtures of wavelengths. A surface reflects some of those wavelengths more strongly than others. Two fabrics can look similar under one lamp but different under another if their reflectance patterns differ. This is one reason museums and manufacturers pay attention to lighting when comparing colors.
Our visual system adds another layer. It adjusts partly to the surrounding illumination, allowing a sheet of paper to look approximately white in several environments. That adjustment is useful, but it does not make all lighting differences disappear. Background colors and nearby objects can also affect the comparison we make.
When an accurate comparison matters, observers use controlled conditions rather than relying on a remembered color from another room. They may place samples side by side under specified illumination. The general lesson is that color appearance emerges from a relationship among the light, the surface and the observer. Describing the surface alone leaves part of the explanation out.

They may reflect different mixtures of wavelengths
They always have identical reflectance patterns
items.explanation: Different reflectance patterns interact with different illumination.

stimulus.title: Why a Species Has Several Names
stimulus.script:
When scientists discuss an organism, the name they use is meant to make communication precise. Yet names can change. A species may be moved into a different group when new evidence reveals relationships that were not understood before. The change is not necessarily a sign that the earlier observers were careless.
Early classifications often relied heavily on visible similarities. Those similarities remain useful, but they can sometimes arise in unrelated organisms facing similar conditions. Genetic evidence may reveal that two organisms that look alike are less closely related than expected. Conversely, organisms that look different may share a more recent ancestor.
Changing a scientific name creates practical work. Museum collections, field guides and research databases may contain the older term. Linking the old and new names helps readers locate previous observations instead of assuming that a renamed organism has no earlier history. Common names present another difficulty because the same everyday name can refer to different species in different places.
The goal of classification is not simply to produce a permanently fixed list. It is to represent relationships in a way that can be revised when evidence improves. Stable communication matters, but so does the ability to correct the account of how organisms are connected.

stimulus.title: How a Footpath Develops
stimulus.script:
On some campuses, a narrow track appears across a lawn even though a paved path runs nearby. The track records repeated choices by people taking a different route. Designers sometimes call such tracks desire paths because they reveal a route people find useful, but the interpretation requires care.
A shortcut may connect two destinations more directly than the planned route. Alternatively, people may avoid the official path because it floods or has poor lighting. Observing the track alone does not tell us which explanation is correct. Interviews and observations at different times can help identify what users are responding to.
There are also users whose needs a track does not represent. A muddy route may be convenient for someone walking quickly but unusable for a wheelchair user. Simply paving every informal path could overlook drainage, safety or accessibility. The decision should consider both the behavior visible on the ground and the people who cannot use that route at all.
So a desire path is evidence, not an automatic instruction. It can reveal a mismatch between a plan and actual use. The useful design response is to investigate the mismatch, understand the constraints and then decide whether to alter the route, improve the original path or provide another solution.
